utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you hear me in a language you understand, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you some questions about your written evidence and the evidence you gave in court earlier this week. Now, my first question is looking at your evidence as a whole, the documents you've also referred to, it's fair to say, isn't it, that during the war you were the UN point of contact with the Bosnian Serb Army for both the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps level as well as headquarters level, the command? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and even -- my contacts were even broader. I also co-ordinated contacts with the civilian structures of our authorities with international organisations and -- and institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, pardon me. In the context of your work and at pages 32428 and 32429 and 32439 of the transcript of your testimony earlier last week, you talked about the meetings you attended with members of the warring factions as well as with the UN, and I want to talk about some of those meetings you were involved in in 1995. Now, in 1995, some of those meetings included meetings in connection with the fall of Srebrenica and the Zepa enclaves in July and August; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of those meetings had to do with these two locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at those meetings, were you aware of the fate of the men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I just want to indicate that it appears that we're proceeding pursuant to Rule 90(H) and I know you have indicated that leading questions are permitted during this process but you also indicated you would be vigilant to ensure that the trial is fair. So I just want to call to your attention at this point that we are now appearing to be proceeding under matters that were not covered in the direct examination nor related to his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, before I engage in any further representations, this discussion is taking place in front of a witness who understands the English language. So if there's going to be submissions, perhaps they should be done outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But this is a matter -- this is a matter of procedural law rather than substance, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and this area which I'm about to discuss is a matter that goes to the witness's credibility squarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you hear my question the first time, Mr. Indjic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I can answer it. There was one single meeting at the level of commander of the Main Staff of the VRS and between him and the UNPROFOR commander at the Jela restaurant, and I attended that meeting. That meeting had to do with Srebrenica. Based on my job or through my job, I was not privy to the events in the course of the operation in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that single meeting that you refer to at the level of commander of the Main Staff in the VRS and UNPROFOR commander at the Jela restaurant, that's the meeting on the 19th of July, 1995, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all this time I cannot really confirm the date with certainty, but the venue of the meeting and the participants, yes. So most probably that is the meeting at issue. And in fact, I was there as an escort to the UNPROFOR commander. I escorted him to the Jela restaurant, and it wasn't even necessary for me to sit there and interpret because the UNPROFOR commander had his own interpreter with him. The meeting had been agreed earlier directly between the office, the liaison office, of UNPROFOR which was at Pale, where an English officer was the liaison officer, and he had agreed this meeting with the command of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that by the date of this meeting, you were unaware.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially I received no information nor was there a need for me to know anything about operation Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So let's have a look at a couple of documents in this regard, and this one probably has an exhibit number at this point which I've omitted to update. It was formerly 65 ter 03727. Sorry, there's no P number. 65 ter 03727, please. And it's about a meeting you had in the afternoon of 13 July 1995 on troop rotation in Zepa, where you said the Security Council's -- thank you. Where you said at paragraph 2 in both languages: " ... the Security Council's Resolution was not reasonable and that it was in fact useless since the Srebrenica pocket was now Serb territory." And if we go over to the next page in both languages, paragraph 7 you added -- pardon me, in B/C/S paragraph -- the third page. You added that you had received orders from Tolimir that contacts with UNPROFOR were to be limited to telephone contacts between Mladic and Janvier. So I just want to have a look at a Security Council Resolution in regard to this document, and that's 65 ter 06202, UN Security Council Resolution 1004. Now, this UN Security Council Resolution at paragraph 3 expresses grave concern at the plight of the civilian population in Srebrenica and condemns the VRS offensive against the safe area. Is that the Resolution you were referring to in the document we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this Resolution before. This is the first time I set my eyes on it. The Resolution I was referring to was the Resolution dealing with the declaration of safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you -- do you remember that Resolution number? Was it 836?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the number. But the gist of what I said was that it was an error to establish safe areas the way they were established. It was an error from the outset, because they were declared safe areas and yet they hadn't been demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on. Now, on the 13th, I want to look at what the rest of the world was talking about or saying and hearing about events in Srebrenica by the 13th of July when you were telling UNPROFOR that Srebrenica was now Serb territory. Could we have a look at 65 ter 2308, please, page 1. Now, on the 13th of July, 1995, you see at page 1 AFP reported the evacuation of Srebrenica refugees continues, Serbs holding male prisoners, and noting at paragraph 2 that draft-age men had been taken to a Bosnian Serb-held town where they could be seen herded into a football ground according to members of a UN convoy. Now, if we could move on to another document of the same date, P2278. It's a report of General Smith on the aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica. And if we can go over to page 2 of this document. At paragraph 3 we see General Smith writing: "The Bosnian Serbs are 'cleansing' Srebrenica. DutchBat are doing what they can to monitor the situation but reports of abductions and murder, unconfirmed as yet, are beginning to be heard. Men of military age are being separated from the refugees." So by the 13th, the date that you were telling UNPROFOR Srebrenica was Serb territory and discussing troop rotation in Zepa, the international media -- pardon me, troop rotation in Zepa and receiving orders from Tolimir, the international media, as well as the UN, General Smith in particular, were concerned about the fate of men from Srebrenica. Your evidence is you didn't know anything about their fate by that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still hold that I didn't -- my position is still that I didn't know anything about it, and I repeat that it wasn't my job. That area was not within my purview.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, before going further, I would like you to explore with the witness the extent of witness's involvement as far as the dialogue, negotiation, whatever, between the Main Staff and the UNPROFOR, because he's a member of the SRK still. So to what extent was he involved in the dialogue between the Main Staff and the UNPROFOR. We heard about it, but it maybe helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I intend to deal with that area through documents as we go through the cross-examination, and that may provide some of the additional information Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I will put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain us the extent of involvement? Do you understand my point of question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking specifically about Srebrenica, Your Honour, and the events in and around Srebrenica, the level of my participation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to know first in general how much were you involved as a liaison officer between the Main Staff of the VRS and the UNPROFOR or international part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain that during the examination-in-chief two days ago. There were two distinct periods, the first period from the outset of the war up until sometime in late 1993 when all the communications went through the group for co-operation with UNPROFOR in Lukavica, a member of which I was as well. Now, after this follows the second period when UNPROFOR established its own office and its own liaison officer in Pale, and an UNPROFOR officer was in that office, and he had direct communication with the Main Staff of the VRS, so that this office, the Lukavica office, in fact remained the office in charge for the level of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and for providing assistance with any meetings that were held at the airport in Sarajevo -- or, rather, meetings in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then you saw the report of -- or interoffice memo of the UNPROFOR which states that in one of its meetings you attended representing -- I don't know in what capacity were you there, but that's the question for you. How come were you involved in that meeting, 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me try to be precise. You mean this meeting with the liaison officer of the Ukrainian Battalion, the documents that relate to the Ukrainian Battalion, or are you referring to the Jela meeting? I just want to be clear on this. I want to avoid any misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where you stated that United Nations Security Council Resolution was unreasonable and now it has become useless. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot -- I do not remember specifically that meeting, but I know that where the Ukrainian Battalion is concerned, because they had frequent troop rotations in Zepa, those rotations and the movements on conveys were agreed via the Lukavica office. In addition to that, the liaison officer of the Ukrainian Battalion frequently went to Lukavica even when he didn't -- when it wasn't on official business --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we upload 3727. Yes. Lukavica, yes. Yes. I was mistaken in terms of its location. It took place in Lukavica. Yes. I'll leave it to you, Ms. Edgerton. Please proceed. Sorry for interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just given evidence that by the 13th, you were unaware. Now, as a humanitarian decorated, as you indicated earlier in the week, for humanitarian work, I take it you yourself would have had concerns as to the fate of these men had you been aware of this information; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a hypothetical question that doesn't make any sense if you ask me. What would have been had it been so? So I don't have any intention of answering that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you been following this trial, Mr. Indjic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some parts of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you familiar with the evidence of Robert Block?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you about him. Robert Block is a journalist who gave evidence here, and he wrote a report on the 17th of July, 1995, about what had transpired with the Muslim men of Srebrenica, and I'd like to show that to you. It's P4397. Now, this is a press report from the "Independent," and it's entitled "Bodies pile up in horror of Srebrenica." And Robert Block reports on video footage from the Serb TV station Studio B that he'd seen of piles of men two feet high, described by the reporter as many dead soldiers. So by the 17th of July, Mr. Indjic, were you aware that there were widespread concerns about the ultimate fate of the men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm surprised that at a serious trial as this one should use newspaper articles, because were it up to newspaper articles you would speak with a dead man now, because "Oslobodjenje" published in 1992 that they had managed to kill me. But to answer your question specifically I have to make a distinction between the two periods. Since the war ended and onwards I learned many things about Srebrenica because I've read numerous documents, but at the time that we're discussing now I had no knowledge as to what was going on in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you were in contact, actually, with General Mladic on the 17th when reports like Mr. Block's were circulating, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you think that General Mladic as the commander had any need to inform me about what was going on? On the other hand, I didn't have any need for any kind of intelligence work vis-a-vis General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd like to explain what you mean when you say, "I didn't have any need for any kind of intelligence work vis-a-vis General Mladic"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite clear. Whoever understand the line of command and control would know that the commander has no need to inform his subordinates about something, particularly not those who are not involved in a particular activity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- may I respond or may I help? The witness responded to what was translated to him in the B/C/S. He was responding to the term "obavijesten," "informed." So I think that the question is -- or the answer is not the answer to the question put. The witness responded to what was translated to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the point was taken by Ms. Edgerton. Would you like to ask again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you actually haven't answered my question, Mr. Indjic. Were you in contact with General Mladic on the 17th when reports like Block's were circulating?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I was in contact with the general at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Maybe I can help you. Can we have a look at D1042. It's a UN report on a meeting with General Smith and President Izetbegovic on the 17th of July, 1995. And if we can go to the next page, paragraph 3, please. Sorry, the page after that. My apologies. Now, this document sets out the text of a message Bosnian authorities asked General Smith to pass to the Bosnian Serb Army, and the message reads: "I have been asked by the Bosnian government, who wish to save their people from further suffering, to elicit from the BSA their conditions for the evacuation of the civilian population of Zepa to Central Bosnia. I now wish to establish contact to discuss this matter at the right level (i.e., Mladic)." And if you skip down to the sixth paragraph on this page, it reads that: "At 5.30, General Smith went to Lukavica Barracks in order to pass the message from the Bosnian government to General Mladic via Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic. The message was passed and Indjic came back with the message that Mladic would personally guarantee the safety of the Bosnian government representatives, and that it was better that they hear the details for themselves." Does this refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one among a hundred conversations that I had during the war with General Mladic as liaison officer. I remember now when I see the document, and I'm glad that we took part in it together so that this problem gets resolved in the most favourable way. I view this as a positive document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember the meeting now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't remember speaking with General Mladic on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a little bit earlier that I spoke with General Mladic at least 100 times, so I cannot provide a decisive answer about a conversation that took place on a specific date, i.e., the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So on the 17th, after -- on the 17th, you were in contact with the Commander-in-Chief of the operation in Srebrenica to pass a message related to the fate of civilians in Zepa, and your evidence is you didn't know anything about the killings of the men from Srebrenica by that date?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still assert that I didn't know anything, and as far as I can see in this document and the conversation, absolutely nothing was mentioned about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And two days after that and since you seem to have trouble recalling the exact date, perhaps we could look at P2280. Two days after that, on the 19th of July, 1995, you were at a meeting between General Mladic and General Smith, and the topics discussed were Srebrenica, the withdrawal of DutchBat, the situation in Zepa, ICRC access to the detainees. You can go over when we have both versions of the document up, I think to page 2. And -- I'm sorry, I don't have the page reference for the B/C/S. And UNHCR access to Srebrenica. So is it your evidence that at this meeting, having spoken to Mladic two days previously, and this meeting which specifically discusses the situation in Srebrenica, that you still didn't know about the killings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a little bit earlier that I came to the meeting as an escort to General Smith. I joined General Smith, and I came to the meeting in Jela in his vehicle. I was present at the meeting, and I returned with General Smith to Lukavica. At no point in time did I have the opportunity nor did I separately alone speak with General Mladic. Not during this meeting. And during this meeting I did not know about any crimes in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on the 21st of July, 1995, again you spoke with General Mladic in the presence of Mr. Harland, and that's at 1D0104. It's a memo from Mr. Harland relating to negotiations at Zepa. Do you disagree? Do you dispute that you spoke with General Mladic actually frequently in that period of time after the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Excuse me, Mr. Indjic. Could we have that 65 ter number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Certainly. 1D0104, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check it out, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've done it again. 1D01014. And apologies to everyone. I had Mr. Reid's handwritten note in front of me with the correct number, and I misread it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 of this document reads that: "At Lukavica Barracks, Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic informed Mr. Harland that he knew nothing of the sector's efforts to broker a local agreement in Zepa." And says of you: "He called General Mladic in my presence. Mladic told him that there was no need for another agreement; that the Bosnian military authorities in Zepa must accept the capitulation agreement made by the ... authorities two days ago; that no international personnel would be allowed into the enclave until the Bosnians began disarming; and that there would [sic] be no evacuation even of wounded and vulnerable individuals until this was done." So this is by the documents your third contact with General Mladic since the fall of Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already responded that during the war, I contacted General Mladic at least a hundred times so that I really cannot say how many times we were in contact in the course of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let me refresh your memory one more time. On the 27th of July, 1995, you interpreted for General Mladic again when he met with General Smith at Boksanica to negotiate the surrender and evacuation of the Muslims in Zepa. By that time did you know about the massacres at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting at Boksanica between General Smith and General Mladic proceeded along the same principles as the meeting at Jela. I accompanied General Smith to Boksanica where the meeting was held, and General Smith had his own interpreter. During that meeting there was no mention of any crimes in Srebrenica. So my answer is that I did not know of any crimes in Srebrenica then either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you a still from a video-clip which was broadcast or taken from a Serb TV broadcast of that meeting, and that still is 65 ter 24460. Now, do you see General Mladic, General Smith, and to the right behind General Mladic, yourself on this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Between General Mladic and General Smith, do you recognise Drina Corps commander Radislav Krstic who was sentenced in April 2004 to 35 years in prison for aiding and abetting genocide in respect of the massacres at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is you attended a meeting with the VRS commander who is presently indicted for the massacres at Srebrenica, and the Drina Corps commander who -- one of the architects of the massacre, and your evidence is you didn't have any information about the massacres at Srebrenica at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by what I said. The meeting in question is a meeting during which the issue of Zepa was discussed. General Krstic was at the meeting because Zepa was in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was compound in nature to a certain extent. Do you agree, Mr. Indjic, that General Krstic was one of the architects of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give an answer to that question because I don't know how the Srebrenica operation was planned and who had what role in that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are tendering only this one? You are not tendering 3727 and 1D1014?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, I intended to deal with these in a line at the end of the cross-examination, and I missed both right now. Maybe I would be better off just doing that, because that's indeed what I had intended on doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, we'll not admit 2308, because -- so we'll admit -- first we'll give the number for -- sorry, I was mistaken. We'll admit 3727. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6083, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll admit 1D1014.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6084, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And this clip will be admitted as Exhibit P6085.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we would appreciate it if the exhibits can be offered as they're discussed so that we can have a better way of -- than our normal practice. After an exhibit is discussed, offered, rather than saving it until the end of the examination. It would be easier if that could be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For my part of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you mean by offer --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: After the document is discussed with the witness that would be the time to tender it as an exhibit rather than accumulating them and trying to deal with them at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That was my point. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: By 22nd of August, 1995, Mr. Indjic, did you know about the killings by then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I knew about that in that period either, because there were no official reports about what had happened at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On 22nd August 1995, you were actually involved in another meeting with General Mladic and General Smith at Borike near Zepa to discuss the withdrawal of British and Ukrainian troops from Gorazde, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember being present at the meeting in Borike, but it was long ago so I cannot really remember what the topic was of the meeting. I remember just that General Mladic took General Smith to see the thoroughbred Lipizzaner horses at Borike.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a video-clip of that meeting and ask you a couple questions about that video-clip. And it's 65 ter number 40576A, we will be starting the video-clip at time-code 1:09 -- 1:09:3. And we don't need any sound for the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've stopped at time-code 1:09:49.3. Do you see General Mladic at this meeting, and do you see yourself now in the image depicted on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who's sitting to your right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recognise who it is. It's not a very clear image. I cannot recognise the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was sitting to your left?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's General Gvero, but perhaps you can rewind it a little bit so that I can be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, what we'll do is we'll go a little bit further in this clip and then I'll ask you some more questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can definitely see that it's not General Gvero but Colonel Milos Djurdjic, who was the liaison officer at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, as far as I can recall. He's deceased, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who is sitting to General Mladic's right on the far side of the interpreter? I mean to General Mladic's left.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who that officer is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. We'll play a further section of the video-clip starting with --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be Kusic, Rajko, Rajko Kusic, the commander of the Rogatica brigade, but I'm not quite sure in this image.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to just go a little bit further in this video-tape and play from time-code 1:11:23.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we're stopping at time-code 1:11:31. Could you tell us who the man is with the moustache sitting at the far end of the table with his face towards us on the left-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. These are members of the Drina Corps with whom I had no official contacts in the course of my duties during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you keep referring to no official contacts, and you've used that word over and over again this morning, and despite the fact that we've seen that you've had a lot of contact, for example, with General Mladic over the course of the month of July 1995 formally and directly, is it your evidence that outside of official contacts you wouldn't have had any conversation with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying. I did not have any conversations with those people because my physical place where I was situated, Lukavica, there was no need for that except for meetings. There was no need for me to go to the areas of any other corps other than the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But we are just seeing here that in July of 1995, you went far and away outside the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because this was an order from General Mladic to come and to accompany General Smith so that he wouldn't go through the territory alone to reach the location of the meeting, to be there as liaison officer and to help them to arrive at the meeting in time. Throughout the time, I am convinced, perhaps, that it would be useful for me to explain again what the role of the liaison officer is, because obviously there is a lack of understanding as to what that role is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe that's something you could do in your redirect examination with Dr. Karadzic. Right now what I'd like to do is look at P1473, a copy of General Mladic's diary for 22 August 1995. And let's go just to pages -- page 310 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before I leave that video-clip, I'd like to tender it, please, Your Honours. Only those specific time-codes given that the witness recognised himself and Colonel Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was wondering whether we need that clip, because there's no transcript. The witness confirmed the participants as far as he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so. Quite so. And let's move on to the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps for the sake of time, we could just dispense with the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is a transcription and translation of General Mladic's notebook dealing with the meeting at Borike on 22 August 1995. At the bottom of the page you see the heading "Meeting with General Smith." And he says: "Present: Smith, John (Colonel) a Colonel accompanying Smith, Captain Tom. "Our side --" not listing you as accompanying or assisting General Smith at all. "Our side: Colonel Djurdjic, Indjic, Kusic, Krunic, Kosoric," and "Suka."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid that I am mentioned as somebody who is on the side of General Smith. Then I would be a traitor. Regardless of whom I came with, I was always a member of my own army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that refresh your memory about the participants in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reason for me not to believe that these people were present, although as for the meeting itself, I do recall that it was held, but I would have difficulty saying anything more detailed about the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General Indjic -- or Colonel Indjic, you've given evidence that you worked in the VRS security organ following the war. Do you remember that? That was in your evidence earlier on this week.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. And before that I was the intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that -- sorry. And working in the intelligence organ, the intelligence centre, and the security -- pardon me, and the security administration of the VRS, you didn't recognise the man with the moustache that identified to you at the end of the table who was actually Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you mention his name, yes, I could confirm that that was him, but before that, I did not recognise him. By the way, let me just explain something to make myself clear. To be an intelligence officer means to gather information on a possible enemy of your state and your people and not collecting information on your own forces and your people. Now, when I was working in the security administration, my job was to prevent the foreign intelligence services from collecting data or information on our own forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Vujadin Popovic is also presently serving a life sentence having been convicted for, and I quote from the decision, "robust participation in the genocide in Srebrenica in 2010." Is it your evidence, given all that we've heard, that by 22 August 1995, you still had no information about the massacres of the men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said earlier. At this time, I did not know about any massacres of any men either because there was no mention of any of it at this meeting itself, and I had no contacts, no personal contacts, with Popovic; and even if I had, I don't see why we would discuss what was going on or had happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Is it your case that the -- the item dealing with this meeting, Mladic's diary's wrong? You didn't mention Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The diary doesn't mention Popovic, but Popovic appears on the film as the witness has just confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the footage again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Reid, could you help us with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, now do you confirm that it was Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall this is Popovic, but as I said, the two of us, we were never anywhere together. We never -- this is perhaps the only time that we attended a meeting together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you identify Kosoric in this clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I mentioned at the outset, I believe that it was Kusic, the person I mentioned as Kusic. That should be Kosoric, the man with the moustache.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is the second of two clips, Your Honour. If you'd like to go back to look at the participants in the first one, we can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just interfere -- intervene in the transcript, please. On page 23, line 11, there was something that was misinterpreted. The witness did not say, "I don't know why we would discuss this." Rather, he said, "I don't know why he would tell me what had happened in Srebrenica." You can check this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Indjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that I don't see any reason why he would tell me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've confirmed that -- or you've stated that by the 22nd -- by that the 22nd of August, 1995, you didn't know anything about the massacres. What about the fact that by that time thousands of men from Srebrenica were missing and unaccounted for? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any official information about the Srebrenica area. Therefore, I had no information about any massacres or any disappearances of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You used that term again, "official information." What about unofficial information? What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot speak about hearsay in such a serious trial as this if I can't recall from whom I had heard something or if I can't be certain about, you know, who told me what. I can only speak about what I know or what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it's hearsay or it's not and -- as to the reliability will be assessed by the -- by the Chamber, you were asked -- you used the term that you didn't know -- you didn't have any official information, and then I was about to put that same question. You were asked by Ms. Edgerton whether you had any unofficial information. Could you tell us as far as you knew at the time, whatever the source of the information that might have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I state with certainty that I had no information, none at all, about any crimes. What I know is that meetings were being scheduled where the issue of prisoners of war were to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was not limited only to crimes. It's also about disappearance or death or whatever. Tell us what you knew about it. Or heard about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is nothing I could say that I knew or heard. Perhaps I saw a TV programme or maybe heard something on the radio, but in the conversations that I had, there was no mention nor any information about any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The word -- there is a word missing here. It should be "in my conversations with officers." That's what's missing. Where he says that perhaps he heard something about it on the radio or on TV, but he didn't hear anything in his conversations with officers. So the word "officers" was missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, now Dr. Karadzic has clarified what you've said and you've limited your sources of information to information with officers. What about your conversations with enlisted men, with soldiers, with intelligence, members of your intelligence community, members of the security organs of your forces? What about those sources? Apart from the officers, what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that there were any conversations, that I had any need or occasion or time to talk about anything that had to do with Srebrenica, because I keep saying, and I have to repeat, Srebrenica was not the subject of my work. It wasn't within my purview.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's go to P898. It's a report on a meeting of 20 July 1995. So that's the day following the meeting you've had with Generals Smith and Mladic where an agreement regarding Srebrenica was struck, and this document is a cable from David Harland regarding a meeting on prisoner exchange and the evacuation of Zepa. Can we go to page 2, please, in both languages. So we see on page 2 that earlier on the 20th, Mladic indicated to Gobilliard that the Serbs would like to hold an immediate meeting on the possibility of a prisoner exchange and that you would have the authority to sign -- to negotiate and sign an agreement on his behalf. So by this time we have evidence that you'd spoken to Mladic on the 17th, the 19th, the 20th, and the 27th of July; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these conversations that were mentioned earlier about my conversations with General Mladic, that's correct, now you reminded me of the dates. But you asked me about these partial conversations. I really can't recall all of them, because I had over 100 conversations with General Mladic. So, yes, I do agree that I did speak with General Mladic at this time, as you reminded me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this document goes on and says that you met with David Harland at 1.30 that afternoon, and you told him that Mladic was willing to make an all-for-all exchange, including the Bosnian soldiers in the Zepa pocket. And then later that day, a meeting took place, a negotiation meeting took place, over the proposal, but there was no final agreement because the Bosnians were not satisfied that Serbs had accounted for all the prisoners taken in the assault on the Srebrenica enclave. So how, Mr. Indjic, was Srebrenica not part of your work?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting dealt with the exchange of prisoners and not Srebrenica. It dealt with the exchange of prisoners on the principle of all for all, which implies the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the subject was not Srebrenica but the exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Even the Bosnian authorities by that point in time, by the 20th of July, 1995, knew that their men in Srebrenica were missing, and you claim you know nothing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still claim that I didn't know anything and that they did know about it. Of course they did. They organised it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by this last remark, "They organised it themselves"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, there was a meeting in Sarajevo between Alija Izetbegovic and the civilian leadership from Srebrenica. The civilian leadership from Srebrenica asked -- requested that Alija Izetbegovic help them resolve the issue, the problem, of Srebrenica. Izetbegovic said, "You had to -- you have to hold out. The Americans want me to show 3.000 dead so that they can intervene." This is information that I gathered from a programme on the Muslim TV in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, fine. Now we understand the source of the last statement that you just made, so we'll move on. Now, I want to go to something David Harland has said. Now, you must remember David Harland, because he was the civil affairs officer and political advisor to UNPROFOR command for a long period of time throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember him. He married a Muslim woman from Sarajevo, thereby showing clearly what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, at page -- pardon me, in P820, paragraph 226, talked about this meeting and the meetings you had with him over Zepa, and he said that it was clear that the Bosnian Serbs wanted to make a deal as quickly as they could. With hindsight, it would appear this was because Mladic realised that the Bosnians knew what had happened in Srebrenica, and he had no chance -- once the Bosnians knew what had happened in Srebrenica, then he would have no chance of getting any Serb prisoners back. The Bosniaks were at this time -- at this time were unsure of what was happening but believed that the offer was some kind of a trick. Mr. Indjic, with everything we've heard, and particularly with your involvement in the negotiations regarding the prisoner exchange, it appears you had precise information regarding the men of Srebrenica and their disappearance. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the case. It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were well informed about the interests of the Bosnian Serb Army at this point in time. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a generalised question. Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that you would attend negotiations and briefings and interpret for General Mladic without being well informed of Bosnian Serb Army interests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you mean when you say Bosnian Serb Army interests. The interests of the Bosnian Serb Army was to end the war. That was our basic interest. That was their basic interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll be -- I'll be more specific. We've now seen, and I'll turn the question a different way, we've now seen evidence of your participation in successive meetings with people who had been indicted and convicted for the genocide of Srebrenica, successive meetings throughout July and August 1995. We've seen information about what the world was reporting about the men at Srebrenica. We've seen information about what the Bosnian authorities knew about the disappearance and massacres of the men at Srebrenica. We've seen articulations of General Smith's concerns, the man that you were involved in the interpretation -- that -- the man for whom you maintain you were interpreting at meetings, and yet your evidence is you knew right up until the end of August 1995 nothing about the disappearance of these thousands of men and their massacre; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to correct you. I have to correct some parts of your speech. First you said that I attended meetings where people who were accused of the crimes in Srebrenica were present. Those people were attended for the -- were accused of the crimes in Srebrenica only after the war. So at those meetings, there were no accused and no one was accused of any crimes. Second, I said very specifically on several occasions that I never interpreted for General Smith. General Smith had his own interpreter, because I don't believe that an Englishman would believe a Serb officer that he was translating correctly his words. The third, I claim that I had no information of any massacre in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. I'd like to move on to a completely different topic, completely different. On paragraphs 166 to 170 -- pardon me. At paragraph 166 of your statement, your written evidence, you referred to a part of a tape of 29 May 1992 of General ordering the shelling of areas in Sarajevo, including Velesici and Pofalici, and you said you listened to it and despite the similarity in voice you had some doubts in. And that's an exert from your testimony in the Galic case in 2003. Now --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. Could you put your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could have a look at 65 ter number 22 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you identify the paragraph number again from his statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will, if you'll just indulge me for yet another moment. And it appears I've got it wrong again, so if I could just pause for a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We may take a break now if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to correct the paragraph citation that I struggled with before our break, the conversation that I wish to direct Mr. Indjic to is at paragraph 116 of his statement, 116.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you recall, Mr. Indjic, when we broke we were talking about the conversation you were commenting on at paragraph 116, dated 29 May 1992, with General Mladic ordering the shelling of Velesici and Pofalici. Now, Mr. Indjic, in 65 ter 22552 which is a transcript of an audiotape recorded interview that General Milovanovic had with the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, in 2001, we can see at pages 137 of the English and 163 of the B/C/S, we can see that General Milovanovic was asked about this specific conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Don't tell me I've got the number wrong again. Your indulgence for a moment. 22552.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm quite happy to read the relevant passage if my obvious weakness with numbers is affecting things. And I'll just speak with Mr. Reid for a moment. Perfect. Thank you. Page 137 of the English. So General Milovanovic spoke about this conversation, noting that it had been on the radio for some time, and he asked Mladic: "Did you really say that?" And Mladic said: "Yes." He explained that he talked to someone on the phone and mentioned that, so he never denied that. And General Milovanovic listened to the conversation, and on the next page -- and you see at the bottom of this page that he recognised Mladic's voice, although the last time he had heard it was three years previously, and on the next page he said: "I presume that's a recording made in 1992." Now, seeing what -- seeing that General Mladic specifically acknowledged to General Milovanovic that it was him in this conversation, are the doubts you expressed in the Galic case now resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say at the beginning that the doubt that was expressed was not from the Galic case, but it was from my interview with Mr. Barry Hogan in 2001. Second, during the time that you were talking, in the first sentence when you were explaining, it was stated or it was written in the transcript that General Milosevic had an interview, so that needs to be corrected, because this is actually a reference to General Milovanovic. I did not say that I doubted whether that was General Mladic. My doubt centred on the fact that the term Velusici was used for the area of town, whereas General Mladic had a family house in that area. So General Mladic knew very well that the name of that area was Velesici, and this is what my doubt was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- so --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I don't have any doubt --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect. So then it seems that if -- if -- it seems that that additional explanation isn't reflected in the statement that you gave which has been filed as your written evidence, then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's reflected or not, but this is my statement given to Mr. Barry Hogan in 2001, and I explained what my doubts were about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another topic. In your testimony earlier on this week in regard to the subject of sniping, you said at T32458, starting from line 2: "The Serb side always expressed its readiness to come to any agreement that would lead to a cease-fire, including an agreement on sniping." And then you were also shown a document by Dr. Karadzic, D2782, dated 18 August 1994, referring to a meeting you were involved in on the 15th regarding -- and the meeting was regarding the implementation of measures arising from the anti-sniping agreement. And you said at 32460 that it implied, this document, implied that there should be a liaison group established that would include both armies and UNPROFOR so that they could respond to any sniping activities quickly, but the group was never established because, as you mentioned Dr. Karadzic: "I believe that the Muslim side was not ready to send its own representative." Now, I'd like to show you a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps account of that very same meeting, and that's P1617. And it's a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command intelligence report to the VRS Main Staff intelligence security sector, dated 15 August 1994, and it -- it details the meeting -- this meeting that you gave evidence about between you, along with Colonel Lugonja and UNPROFOR, concerning the implementation of the anti-sniping agreement. And it sets out in this first paragraph UNPROFOR's plan which you see at paragraph 1 at the bottom of the English page. And if you go over to page 2 in English, it sets out at paragraph 1 on page 2 according to General Tolimir's instructions the VRS proposal. Now, at paragraph 2, we see the VRS proposal is -- or reads: "... we cannot accept anti-sniper units which would operate on the respective side because it's not part of UNPROFOR's mandate, and a joint staff is not necessary because elaborate instruments of mutual information already exist." Now, in regard to the same situation we're discussing, I want to go over to P862 next, which is a letter dated 17 August 1994 from Colonel Gausseres, who was the Sector Sarajevo Chief of Staff to Colonel Lugonja, and that reads in paragraph 2, second sentence: "On your request there will be no anti-sniping teams on your side but you are expected not to retaliate if you do not want to worsen an already very tense situation." So, Colonel Indjic, a document from your own forces which is in part confirmed by this UNPROFOR document shows that it was -- not only did the Serb side object to UN anti-sniping teams on their territory, but they specifically refused the joint commission which is completely contrary to the evidence you gave earlier this week, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have never seen these documents before. I'm seeing them for the first time. Secondly, I expressed my opinion why the agreement as not implemented. And thirdly, it's absolutely clear to me that anti-sniper teams would not be accepted because this was beyond the UNPROFOR mandate, and any acceptance of going beyond the mandate would imply going even further beyond the mandate. As for the documents, I'm seeing them for the first time. I don't doubt that they exist. And in my conversation with President Karadzic, I voiced my opinion as to why the agreement was not respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: President Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic, asked you: "Do you know anything, lieutenant-colonel, about why this never materialised, which side was blocking it?" And your answer was: "I believe that the Muslim side was not ready to send its own representative."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I expressed my opinion, my opinion as to what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And these documents completely contradict your expressed opinion, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that it's completely contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll move on --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that is discussed here is the modality of the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, this Chamber's heard evidence that from the end of July until the 14th of August, 1994, there was a series of abortive meetings regarding the possibility of an anti-sniping agreement mainly abortive because of the lack of interest in an agreement by Tolimir and Sarajevo-Romanija Corps liaison officer Colonel Indjic, who obstructed the negotiations. The Serb negotiators would find excuses to avoid doing even the slightest -- pardon me, the easiest things that could be done to prevent sniping, such as installation of line of site barriers. That evidence, Mr. Indjic, is completely consistent with the document from your own corps as well as the UNPROFOR document we've just looked at, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is really not clear to me what you are talking about in what you have just said. You mentioned General Tolimir, myself, obstructions, while it's clear from everything that General Tolimir said that this is only a matter of the mode of implementation of the agreement, and I don't know what kind of obstruction is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll go on to another topic, and it's about your role in the hostage taking which you discussed at paragraph 191 of your statement. Pardon me, 171, 171. And you said there in paragraph 171, and I assume it relates to May of 1995, that on the basis of an order, you personally informed the French at Lukavica Barracks that the Serb side considered them war prisoners and they had the right to keep their pistols. So, first of all, when you talk about the French at Lukavica Barracks, I presume you're referring to French peacekeepers who had been posted to the weapons collection point at Lukavica barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean members of the French battalion who were part of the Sector Sarajevo UNPROFOR force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the events you describe in paragraph 171, your actions, was that -- did those take place before or after you ordered them surrounded and fired at them with RPGs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please specify which events you are talking about, whether they happened before or after.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could -- if you look at the screen in front of you, you see the evidence you gave in paragraph 171, and what I want to know is did that happen before or after you ordered them surrounded and your forces fired two RPGs at them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to avoid misunderstandings, I'm going to take some time and describe the events as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- through the operations officer --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, my question was did this happen before or after the two RPGs were fired at them? So it's a kind of a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what happened before or after. Can you tell me specifically what it is that you are asking me that happened before or after?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at 65 ter 24480. And that's an Associated Press article dated 26 May 1995, entitled "French UN platoon surrenders to Bosnian Serbs." And if you go down to the fourth paragraph on this page, it reads: "An Associated Press reporter watched Serbs take over 21 French soldiers who had been guarding Serb guns turned over to the UN at this barracks in a Serb-held suburb of Sarajevo. "A Serb officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic, first tried to coax the French into surrender and entered the UN headquarters [sic] unarmed to negotiate. The French commander said he had orders not to surrender." This article says you then ordered military police to take positions and prepare to fire. For three minutes, automatic rifle fire targeted the building where the 21 French men were. The commanding Serb officer said hold fire and watch for the white flag. No flag appeared. Two rocket propelled grenades hit a truck and an APC and minutes later the French surrendered without firing a shot. Does this help you with the sequence of events and clarify what happened before and after?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all of this. I know more about it than you do, but I am not sure. I don't know what you are trying to ask me, what happened before and what happened afterwards. There is one very important sentence missing here, and that is when I was inside the building with the French officer unarmed, since he did not have orders to surrender, we agreed that we would fire at vehicles without jeopardising the lives of his men with that, and then when the fire stopped, then he would come out with a white flag and surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, in fact, this article and your testimony supplement the information that you gave in your written evidence at paragraph 171; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6086, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the year prior to this event when your forces detained around 150 UN personnel following the air-strikes against Serb forces at Gorazde in April 1994, and to do that I'd like us to have a look at 65 ter 19302, a report on the detention of Lima HQ and teams from 14 April 1994 to 19 April 1994. And the drafter of this is Shaun Heintz, UNMO, Shaun Heintz. Page 1 of this document says -- in fact, it's the very second sentence on page 1 which says: "An order was issued from the HQ at Lukavica by LO Major Indjic that all UNMO teams were to be confined to their accommodation." And then if we go over on the next page, bottom of page 2, Heintz reports -- I'll just make sure I can see it on this page, and I do have the page right. Your indulgence for a moment. If we could go over to the -- ah, no, it is at the bottom of page 2. Thank you. Page 2. At the bottom of page 2, Heintz reports on a meeting you had with him on the 18th of April where you said because of the bombing on the 16th, you were expecting the order to kill one UNMO. So a year before the hostage-taking in May 1995, you also ordered the detention of UN personnel in April 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Crucially -- in its crucial points it's incorrect because from my position I'm not able to order anything. I can convey somebody's order, act pursuant to somebody's order, but I myself cannot issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under whose orders were you acting when you relayed this order to detain the UN personnel at Lukavica in April 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot specifically say who was the duty operations officer at that time, but all the orders proceed along the command and control line via the operations duty officer. I wished that I was able to read the document in its entirety, because all I'm being shown here are parts of a document which do not constitute a whole. I wish I had been given the opportunity to read it in my native language regardless of the fact that I am familiar with English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am not sure if we have a B/C/S version. We will print out these eight pages and provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also said at paragraph 171 with regard to May 1995, that the first group of UNPROFOR soldiers was captured by individuals without orders, plans, or co-ordination to do so. When was that first group captured?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a misunderstanding here when it says an UNPROFOR group. What is being discussed here are military observers, UNMOs, who are in separate observation posts. Before, in any case -- this happened before the capture of the French soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to tell you. It's been a long time since then. But I know that this happened before the capture or the arrest of the French soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, where?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, it has to do with the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What group do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the individuals, the military observers, UN military observers who were part of the United Nations who were deployed at isolated observation posts, the so-called Lima posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now shall we pause and give him the time to read this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And this relates to the 1994 issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, while we're pausing on this point, if I could, assuming that this is evidence that's going to the credibility of the witness since it's related to events that are not part of the -- the 1994 detentions are not part of the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to state it's my understanding that this is not 90(H) evidence but this is related to credibility because this is not something that was covered in the statement or the examination-in-chief, the 1994 detentions of UN personnel in response to the Gorazde incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, he talked about UN prisoners of war in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I believe that that was related to 1995, but if you're interpreting it more broadly perhaps that's fair, but in any event, it seemed like that that was related to the -- count 11 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It goes squarely again to his credibility, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And just on a related point since the witness is still reading, when it comes to the time when the allotted time for cross-examination has expired, I think it's important for the Chamber to consider how much time we have spent on issues that were not contained in the statement that are purportedly relating to credibility. It seems like we still haven't really gotten to the core issues of the Sarajevo component of our case and almost the whole two hours has been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informed by the Registrar that the Defence, Mr. Karadzic, used for his examination-in-chief 2 hours and 36 minutes, and Prosecution has used so far one and a half hours. So she has still half --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One and 45 minutes, not one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm sincerely hoping that this time the witness takes reading a document that he's already commented on is not counting against the allotted time that the Prosecution has, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you done your reading, Mr. Indjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have to read on. It's not a problem. I'm also quite grateful that you gave me a document to work with since on the screen what I see right now is a very important paragraph, paragraph 2, specifically, on my screen telling us why the military observers were grouped in a single location for their personal safety during the NATO air-strikes. They were allowed to use the phone to get in touch with their superiors and to ask to have food and other necessities shipped in, meaning there was no mistreatment or harassment whatsoever. And it was precisely in order to avoid any random individual incidents against the NATO staff. They were all grouped in a single location. We decided to do that so that we would keep these people apart from their signals equipment so that they could not use it in order to guide NATO aeroplanes to their targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I've actually left 1994 some time ago, and we were dealing with questions relating to the matters that were discussed in your statement at paragraph 171, and that's the situation in May 1995. Now, you spoke a couple of times regarding mentioning the French soldiers. I take it you're referring to the French soldiers who were taken hostage during the attack on Vrbanja Bridge on the 27th of May of that year.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not the French soldiers that I have in mind, because these French soldiers, as far as I can recollect, were taken prisoner by one of the parties to the conflict, same as a number of VRS soldiers were taken prisoner by the French battalion, and they were being held at Sarajevo airport where the French battalion was stationed. So it's a question of prisoners of war on both sides of the conflict, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you just on that line document P2434, which is a letter from UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo Commander Gobilliard to Dragomir Milosevic, dated 3 June 1995. And it refers to you, and it says -- it talks about how a French officer was forced to kneel in the street with his hands tied behind his back and with a gun at his head while Serb soldiers threatened to shoot him if the UNPROFOR troops refused to withdraw from the OP, observation post, and then it stays that: "Additionally, during the retaking of the position that morning, Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic spoke to one of my officers on the telephone and said, 'If you don't stop the attack immediately, I will kill one of the French soldiers.'" Now, you talked earlier this week and in your written evidence about the protests that were sent to your office. Is this a protest that you would have received about your own specific behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a report. It's not a protest. As for the allegations about me making that statement over the phone, that is a blatant lie. I am sufficiently trained and a sufficiently skilled professional to know that were I to go on and say something like that, I certainly wouldn't do it over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How would you do it then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't do it at all, madam. It goes against the grain of everything that I was taught, that prisoners were to be treated in keeping with the Geneva Conventions and prisoners were not to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. I'd like to go on, now that we're talking about Sarajevo, to the subject of demilitarising Sarajevo, and you talked about this in your evidence earlier this week. During your testimony, first of all -- actually, let me ask you this question: You would agree that on 9 February 1994, the Bosnian Serb Army and the ABiH agreed to a cease-fire, the establishment of a total exclusion zone in Sarajevo, the interposition of UNPROFOR between the two sides, and the placement of heavy weapons in weapons collection points, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree [Realtime transcript read in error "disagree"] with everything you said apart from the date. I can't quite recall the date before I've been shown the relevant document, but everything you said about the actual activities is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at the relevant document. That's P827, a UN civil affairs weekly political assessment by Viktor Andreev.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to enter a correction to something I said before. The transcript says "I disagree," whereas I said "I agree" with everything you said apart from the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. If we could go over to page 2 of this document, this notes under the heading Sarajevo second bullet point negotiating in the shadow of a NATO threat, the Bosnian Serb Armies have made an oral agreement for the Greater Sarajevo. The agreement, which came into effect on the 10th of February, has four main elements and goes in to describe the elements. Now, if we can just flip back over to page 1. I apologise. Could we go back over to page 2, please. My apologies. So page 2 of this document, in the first paragraph under the second bullet point makes the date of these events quite clear. Would you be prepared to agree that the agreement we're talking about reflects an oral agreement between the two parties which is to come into effect on the 10th of February?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that all these activities were carried out. Now, was this an oral agreement or actually one that was signed black and white, I'm sorry, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. I asked you whether the agreement was something which was to come into effect on the 10th of February.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't recall the specific time line, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're disagreeing with Mr. Andreev's report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would need to go through the entire report in order to be able to agree or indeed disagree. I can't judge this report portion by portion, as it were, and not as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, keeping in mind that we have limited time for this, I'm going to move on to another point. You --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask for a reference. Where does the document actually claim that it was to take effect on the 10th? In the third paragraph in the English [In English] "The armies were given ten days to withdraw 20 kilometres, and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, if I am, as everybody says, to be strictly limited to this time. Dr. Karadzic has seen this document and he has seen the reference in the second bullet point, 10th of February. If we could move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony at 32448, you discussed P1641, dated 10 February 1994. Now, that was a proposal for setting aside artillery from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander to the VRS Main Staff. And Dr. Karadzic asked you whether this proposal, which was from General Milosevic, was accepted and implemented, and you said, "I know that it wasn't," and that was at T24439. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
