utterances.text: I remember the proposal talked about using military cunning and to place some of the nonfunctioning weapons into the reserve, but that proposal by the Main Staff was not complied with as proposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at P847, which is dated 9 February 1994. And it's an order of the VRS Main Staff from General Milovanovic on bringing artillery weapons from around Sarajevo -- pardon me, on bringing artillery weapons around Sarajevo from the Hercegovina Corps and the Drina Corps, and it says under paragraph 1: "In the course of today and tomorrow the command of the SRK shall move artillery from other positions towards Sarajevo, mainly inoperative weapons, which will be put up at the appropriate firing positions around Sarajevo. The commanders of the Herzegovina and Drina Corps shall put the inoperative weapons unconditionally at the disposal of the commander in order to disguise our intentions." So the proposal which you say was not implemented on reading this document is obviously a proposal on the implementation of this order from General Milovanovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, there are some discrepancies here in terms of time. This order by General Milovanovic - and I've never seen it before - is dated the 9th of February, and the proposal is dated the 10th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic. Mr. Indjic, that's completely unresponsive to the question I asked you. The question I asked you was: The proposal which you say wasn't implemented is, on reading this document, obviously a proposal for the implementation of this order from General Milovanovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the order. However, I know what was placed under UNPROFOR's control. In all of the UNPROFOR documents, you have lists telling you exactly what types of artillery weapons, what exactly was placed under control. It was all of the artillery that was available to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that ended up being placed under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Uh. So as I understand your evidence, the answer -- actually, I don't understand that you've answered my question, but we'll move on. Let's have a look at 65 ter 09150. It's a document dated 12 February 1994, from General Milovanovic to the corps commanders, confirming that the apparent -- that the apparent withdrawal of heavy weapons isn't actually a withdrawal and surrender, but, rather, a manoeuvre of these weapons into various places around Sarajevo. So not only does this document confirm the document that we've just spoken about, P00847, it confirms the document you discussed, P1641, General Milosevic's proposal was being effectively implemented. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the case. I'm saying that all of the artillery weapons that were part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were placed under control. It was necessary because of the fear felt by the soldiers to explain to all the men that this wasn't about surrendering their artillery weapons. It was necessary to explain to them that the weapons were still around, but none of the weapons remained outside UNPROFOR control, fully functional or broken. It didn't really make any difference. All of the artillery weapons were placed under their control. I think the essence of what really matters is what actually happened on the ground and not necessarily just the accompanying documents. So what happened in actual reality on the ground is all of the artillery weapons were placed under effective control.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right then. Let's have a look at some documents from your forces that I think you would probably agree reflect what actually happened on the ground. Could we have a look, please, at P6016.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may this document that we just looked at be admitted? I think it would be useful for that -- to understand the context and explain his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. My omission. Could this be a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6087, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So P6016 that you see on the screen in front of you is a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command document with a list of technical and materiel equipment that has not been pulled out, and it's broken down by brigade. Now, if you go down this list, you see, Mr. Indjic, the Rajlovac Brigade has not pulled out a 40-millimetre gun, a T-55 tank. The 3rd Sarajevo Brigade hasn't pulled out a T-55 tank and a 122-millimetre howitzer along with some mountain guns. The Ilijas Brigade hasn't pulled out a 122-millimetre mortar and two T-55 tanks. So, Mr. Indjic, we could go down through this list, but this list contradicts what you've just said in your testimony to the effect that all the artillery weapons were placed under effective control.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite obvious from the document that we're talking about, the 21st of February. I have never seen this document before. I don't know what was happening up and down the chain of control and command. There may have been some initial attempts to avoid placing all the artillery weapons under control, because this was the initial stage where these weapons were being regrouped, so to speak, and there was a lot of mistrust. I stand by my previous statement. Finally all the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps artillery was placed under UNPROFOR control.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you're now qualifying your previous statement, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm qualifying my previous statement because I was not myself part of the control and command chain. This is a report by the brigades to the corps command. I was no party to this. I did know about the check-points and the control that was conducted there, where the weapons ended up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Indjic, among the documents that you discussed in your testimony earlier this week, you indicated that you were part of a committee with a view to establishing and ensuring the weapons collection points and moving the weapons into those areas, and you're now saying you weren't part of the command and control chain in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'll try and find the precise citation in a moment, Your Honours. That was at T3 -- pardon me. That was at T32420.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said: "I'm absolutely familiar with that. I was personally involved in co-ordinating these activities in terms of pulling out anti-aircraft weapons." And further --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll have to take a moment to find the citation, Your Honour, given the witness's answer. Your indulgence. We'll find the citation, because we all remember it, Your Honour, but I wonder if Your Honours will allow for the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not 32420, line 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's one of them. We're looking for the comment with respect to an associated exhibit now, Your Honour. We found it now, Your Honours. Your indulgence. The cite is 32452.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Indjic, you were asked by Dr. Karadzic, were you familiar with the progress of the negotiations and how all these things were being implemented regarding the exclusion area, the total exclusion area? And your answer was: "Yes I was a member of the delegation doing the negotiations and was personally in charge of co-ordinating activities regarding the grouping of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all true as stated. I stand by that. I was involved in the negotiations. Locations were determined where the heavy artillery weapons would be collected. I co-ordinated all of the activities in relation to that. UNPROFOR's arrival, weapons control, the drawing up of lists, I don't see what's open to challenge there. If there was a ruse somewhere between the corps commanders and the brigade commanders going on, I wasn't interested in that. My job was to determine whether someone was hiding weapons or not. My job was not to do that. My job was to control the actual collection of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go, before leaving this topic, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, just for planning purpose, you passed two hours a while ago. How much longer do you need for your cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Twenty minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And then for the record, could you scroll back to -- oh, yes. Page 48, line 8. When you referred to transcript page 24439, I take it it should read 32449.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, indeed. And my sincere apologies. This has been a problem for months, and I'm particularly afflicted today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please try to finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you talked in your evidence yesterday -- pardon me, earlier in the week about the removal of anti-aircraft guns from around the area of the airport. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not just guns but anti-aircraft weapons, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then let's have a look at P1650 [sic], and it's a document from General Milosevic on the camouflaging of heavy weapons in the 20-kilometre zone around Sarajevo, and it's dated 21 August 1994, 1670. 1670, please. Now, this document talks about four Bofors anti-aircraft guns which were located at firing positions on the MUP roof in Ilidza, and it reports on General Rose's warning to General Milosevic to stop shooting at UN planes with those guns and notes that they haven't been removed despite previous warnings and orders - if we go over to page 2 in the English we see the order displayed in the B/C/S - and orders that they be removed to new firing positions where they will be camouflaged and sheltered from air and ground recon. So it seems, Mr. Indjic, that the anti-aircraft weapons that you talked about in your evidence earlier this week that were removed in 1992, in fact, weren't removed at all and weren't removed following the establishment of the total exclusion zone and weren't going to be removed but were going to be camouflaged to prevent further identification by UN forces, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. I think there's a general confusion of concepts here. My statement about the withdrawal of anti-aircraft weapons was about surrendering control over Sarajevo airport to UNPROFOR. That's what it was about. So as part of this withdrawal effort, check-points were toured in Sokolac and further afield, locations that the weapons had been taken to. If you think that four Bofors guns are all the anti-aircraft artillery weapons available to a corps-level military unit, then I'm afraid you don't know much about the military. I'm not trying to conceal anything. I'm not going to whether anyone actually tried to conceal these four weapons. They may well have. But I know what my job was, co-ordinating the artillery withdrawal activities in keeping with the agreement. Now, was there someone who failed to obey these orders? I don't know, but I think the best thing for you would be to take it up with that person. It wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. I'm going to -- I have two more questions for you -- no, actually two small areas. In today's transcript, at page 7, line 21, you responded to Judge Kwon's questions explaining your roles during the first period of the war, liaising with UNPROFOR in respect of the VRS in its entirety, and from late 1993 onwards, liaising with UNPROFOR and providing assistance only as regards the SRK area of operation. But, in fact, as we've now seen, you were regularly called on to assist and advise and interpret for General Mladic and other members of the Main Staff. You were a member of multiple commissions at different times, including mixed working group commissions between the UN and the VRS, the State Commission for prisoners of war. You participated in the negotiations of the total -- relating to the total exclusion zone, the anti-sniping agreement, the withdrawal from Igman and Bjelasnica, negotiations for the restoration of utilities, and you were negotiated -- or, pardon me, you were authorised to negotiate and sign the agreement on prisoner exchange in Zepa. So, actually, isn't this a more accurate depiction of your true role within the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am grateful to you for showing this, and I am really proud now of the time that I spent in the Army of Republika Srpska, because I -- I've almost forgotten all the good things that I've done there, and I believe that this reflects the actual truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did all those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I apologise for interrupting you. Now, one last question -- series of questions. Earlier this week you talked about your duties when the war was over and we talked about them briefly today, and the reference earlier this week is T32415. You said you became a member of the 410th Intelligence Centre and after leaving that, you were with the security administration of the General Staff of the VRS until your retirement. So could you tell me the period of time you worked in the 410th Intelligence Centre and the security administration?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked at the 410th Intelligence Centre from the end of the war up until 2001, and I worked at the security administration from 2001 until my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And in that context, it's correct, isn't it, that you would work together with Colonel Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Colonel Ljubisa Beara was in charge of the security organ during the war, and as an intelligence officer, I belonged to the 410th Intelligence Centre. I know that it's hard for you to understand this, but there is intelligence work and counter-intelligence work, and Colonel Beara was in charge of counter-intelligence and had no connecting points with me. Now, as for the security administration, at the time it wasn't Colonel Beara anymore but, rather, General Lugonja who was at its head.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter 24466, and it's a document dated October 1996, in the VRS Main Staff sector for intelligence and security affairs security department. 24466.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is released, Your Honours. The speed at which the system works sometimes defeats us. And this is the last two questions, Your Honour. All right. I can deal with the Serbian version on the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document reports on a meeting you attended with Beara and Mr. Latapi. Now you've just said that you had no connections with Beara. This document shows the contrary. Did you have any connection with Beara during the course of your work, any connection, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained, because you asked me about my service at the 410th centre and the administration -- security administration. Had you asked me who Colonel Lafet [phoen] was, I would tell you that he was a French intelligence officer, although the French would have a problem with that because he was there as a French defence ministry person, but my work was as an intelligence officer and that has nothing to do with whether I had anything to do with Beara. Would you like now us to go into some of the intelligence operations and investigations that were done? Would you like me to testify here as an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. My question is whether or not you had connection with Beara, and even though you were at a meeting together with him as seen in this document, you -- you maintain that you did not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended a meeting with Latapi together with Beara, and specifically I had dealings with Latapi and not with Beara.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 65 ter 04416. And that, Mr. Indjic, is a statement that General Milovanovic gave in writing to the RS government, dated September 2004. And if we can go over to page 3 in both languages, second paragraph on page 3 referring to the period at the beginning of 1997, we see General Milovanovic says: "General Mladic stayed in Crna Rijeka with his security guards who were supposed to protect him from being arrested by The Hague Tribunal. In the beginning the commander of that powerful security group was Colonel Ljubisa Beara." So I'd like to put it to you, Mr. Indjic, that actually your answer that you've just given is trying to distance you from Colonel Beara in light of his involvement in protecting General Mladic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I -- I'm not trying to distance myself. Quite the contrary, I'm sorry I did not personally take part in providing security to General Mladic. I wasn't given the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we take a break before you start your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although we have a witness, before doing so, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling. I refer to the Prosecution's motion to exclude tu quoque evidence of Witness Srdjan Sehovac filed on the 18th of January 2013, and the accused's response to that motion filed on the 22nd of January, 2013. The Chamber has reviewed the draft statement of Srdjan Sehovac which bears 65 ter number 1D6070 in light of the Prosecution motion and the accused's response and finds that the answers to questions 2, 3, 9 the last sentence only, 13, 15 to 18 inclusive, 23, 24, 35, 36(A)(c), 36(A)(d) of the statement which the Prosecution seeks to exclude falls within the category of detailed evidence pertaining to crimes committed against Bosnian Serbs which the Chamber has consistently excluded on the grounds that it is irrelevant tu quoque evidence. Further, the Chamber also considers that the answers to questions 8, 20, and 28 of the statement are not relevant to the charges against the accused in the indictment. The Chamber therefore grants the motion and excludes the answers to questions 2, 3, 8, 9, in case of para 9, last sentence only, 13, 15 to 18 inclusive, 20, 23, 24, 28, 35, 36(A)(c) and 36(A)(d) of the statement and will not admit the associated exhibits referred to therein. The accused is ordered to upload a redacted version of Srdjan Sehovac's statement which reflects this decision. We'll break for -- before doing so, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I'm at the Court's disposal with respect to this but I wanted perhaps to raise a scheduling issue that the Court might want to be -- to consider during the recess because I think would certainly arise by the end of the day. So it's just a very -- I can alert the Court to the nature of the problem before it recesses if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I know that, particularly in respect of this matter but in respect of related matters, the Court has tried to leave scheduling in the hands of the parties to the extent possible, but this is one matter which requires the Court to resolve, and it concerns the timing of the commencement of the cross-examination for Mr. Milosevic. The background to this issue, of course, is -- has been previously discussed in court and includes the absence of a draft statement or a 65 ter summary, the belated and recent provision of a kind of substitute for the 65 ter summary which itself had deficiencies and was topical in nature to a large degree, the belated and recent provision of a list of documents to be used, half of which were not translated at the time it was provided and so on, and I think these issues were described in somewhat more detail in court earlier. Now, the Defence position very correctly, and one which has been appreciated, has been that there is indeed a notice problem and that as a result it would willingly accommodate the Prosecution with whatever time was reasonably needed before commencing cross, and this has been the Defence's position even before we came to court and was, I think, expressed in court on Monday as well. Of course sometimes the devil is in the details and in discussion yesterday with the Defence we advised of the period of time that we considered under these circumstances appropriate before the commencement of cross and indicated that we would wish five working days after the conclusion of his cross before we commenced. The Defence responded that it considered commencing on Monday in light of the -- in light of the weekend to be reasonable. In -- in our view, that means there was no accommodation since that's commencing in the normal course of business but, more importantly, it doesn't reflect the circumstances here in a -- in a fair manner. Now, we never considered that the understanding was that there was an acknowledgement that the Defence would agree to whatever time it deemed reasonable. We thought it would be a more objective reasonable test, but nevertheless we tried to find a workable middle ground. That wasn't successful. The Defence adhered to the view that commencing immediately after cross, if it concluded, for example, on Monday, would be sufficient. Under these circumstances, we are trying to adjust as much as reasonably possible bearing in mind that to some extent reasonableness can differ in the minds of people, but -- so we are only seeking the most modest of accommodations which mean the following: That we are asking that assuming the cross-examination ends today, which I doubt is the case, that the -- that the direct examination ends today, that the cross-examination would commence on Wednesday, and if it ended on Monday, unless it was only a very brief portion of Monday, that the cross-examination would commence on Thursday. That is two days in between. So that's our position, Mr. President. I thought it best to advise you of the circumstances that had arisen so that the Court could be considering it before the conclusion of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably now you understand how much pause you should put between the question and answer. The French translation has been only now completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise to the translators, in particular to Judge Lattanzi, and that was a painful way -- I think hopefully the lesson is embedded, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly on this. We obviously agree on the concept and normally we agree on what's reasonable, but in this particular case we believed that since they had all the material on last Sunday, that by commencing their cross-examination on Tuesday they would have had basically eight or nine days since they got the material to prepare for the cross-examination, and we thought that was enough. But if you disagree, we will accommodate whatever you order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What are you proposing us to do during those two days in the interim, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, maybe I take him off the hook a little bit there. We do have three witnesses that will be here proofed on Sunday and could testify in that period if the Chamber ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're prepared to proceed on those witnesses, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have no difficulty with conducting cross-examination of those three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If -- unless something unexpected happens with their proposed testimony in between, no, we don't have any. We're prepared to proceed on cross-examination of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider your submission and come back to you in due course. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In regard to your request, Mr. Tieger, the Chamber sees no difficulty with accommodating it, but speaking for myself, I would like to be able to -- we could start with cross-examination immediately following the evidence of those three witnesses, but it would -- but I'm not sure how long it will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think about a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's almost two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tieger, would it be possible? But shall we leave it there and see how it evolves?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's best, Mr. President, at this point, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that ensures hard working on the part of Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we begin, I just need to ask for both of us to keep in mind the necessity of breaks or pauses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that I wanted to say, Mr. President, that Madam Edgerton is probably the reason for the generosity in granting this time. If you recall, the Prosecution had a large story when we asked for the postponement of Witness Skiljevic. We urge -- or, are in favour of flexibility, and we believe that the process should be mutual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, today on page 50 of the transcript, in response to allegations that we avoided pulling the weaponry out and the handing over of those weapons for the UN to monitor, you will recall that this did happen. Do you remember when the agreement was signed to group the weapons and place it under monitoring?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot bring into my memory the date. I know that I looked at the agreement, that it exists, but I cannot recall the date. It's not coming into my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 1D26670 in e-court, please. It's possible that parts of this document have already been tendered under different numbers, but this document should be viewed as a single document consisting of two parts. Is this the document that you thought you saw, that being the agreement to place the weapons under monitoring and regarding the unrestricted movement of UNPROFOR verification patrols?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was shown to me by the Defence. It was signed at the top level and I know that after this document organisational orders ensued as to the way in which this can be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is the date? When was this agreement concluded? When was it signed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19 February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the date again.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah. It was signed on the 18th and was meant to go into effect on the 19th. In the paragraph -- the first paragraph it states that it is to be effective from 1200 hours on the 19th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was this followed by any kind of verbal agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After this date, the 18th or the 19th of February, 1994, were there any proposals or suggestions from General Milosevic or Milovanovic about not respecting or about evading this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we saw what was written on the 9th. Do you have any information, knowledge, or any document indicating that after the signing something similar was asked?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe. I don't think that can be put in any other way. I don't know. I don't have an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at page 2 of the document, please. Do you remember this protocol of implementing -- can we look at the last page, please, so that we can look at the date. What is the date here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back to the previous page, page 2 of the document, please. Can you please tell us in relation to paragraph 1, which states in the event that UNPROFOR withdraws for any reason from mutually agreed sites without out agreement, what would be the rights to our weapons in that case or in the event of Muslim attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, it states that in such a case, the Army of Republika Srpska reserves the right to redeploy its weapons and increase troop levels on the front line; while in the event of a Muslim attack on the Serbs, which UNPROFOR is not able either to prevent or stop immediately, the BSA reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the UNPROFOR prevent a single attack by the Muslim forces on the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR did not prevent any attack, and I think that that is understandable, because the general mandate of UNPROFOR was that it could not use force except in the case of self-defence, defence of its own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the UNPROFOR ever call upon NATO to protect the Serbian side by bombing Muslim positions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such information, and as far as I know, this did not happen, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the condition from paragraph 2 that UNPROFOR must return to Igman from where we withdrew in August 1993, actually, that the Muslims should withdraw and the UNPROFOR should return.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was part of the demilitarisation agreement pertaining to Igman and Bjelasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 6 where it states that neither the Muslim or the Serb side will be allowed to extract military advantages during the current pacification process in the Sarajevo district? Did the Serb side extract any advantage and did the Muslim side respect this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is also leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the sides adhere to the conditions stated in paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our side pulled out its heavy weaponry, fulfilling the conditions set in the paragraph, and there was also the respect of the cease-fire. That was also secured.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This has been admitted. Do you have an exhibit number, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page 1 is P1820 and it's also page 1654. And we all recognise the other pages as having been previously admitted. We just have to track down the numbers, but they were Prosecution exhibits. Sorry, they were Defence exhibits during the cross-examination of a Prosecution witness. D717, possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. If necessary, we'll come back to this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D01658, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that in the Serbian it was collated erroneously, so the second page should be the first page. Without reading through the document, can you please tell us how the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps acted already on the 18th of February in view of the Karadzic-Akashi agreement going into effect of the 19th of February? What does it state here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an operative order pursuant to the agreement where the regrouping of weapons are provided for as covered under the agreement in connection with the demilitarisation of Sarajevo. We're talking about materiel and equipment of 12.7 millimetres and over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the page -- the first page in the Serbian. Actually, can we look at the last page in both versions where we can see the signature line with the signature of Galic, and can I ask you to read the first sentence at the top of the page and to tell us what sanctions the violators would be subject to.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order precisely defines that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. One page prior to this English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pages are not the same in the Serbian and the English, if that's means anything to you. In the Serbian, the order precisely defines that in the event of finding hidden weaponry, the commanders would be subject to all criminal, moral, and material responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And does the order encourage or prompt any kind of evasion of the agreement or the order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite the opposite. It orders the consistence -- consistent respect of the agreement and threatens sanctions in the event that it is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems that we're not looking at the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The wrong document has been uploaded. This document only has five paragraphs. This seems to be the translation of 1D01659, and we need 58. The translation that we see is the translation of document 1D01659. Can this previous document be tendered, and if there is no translation, then perhaps the document can be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I lost that somewhere. What was the number of the document we are seeing in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's 1D01658.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And the translation -- yes. I don't think we have the correct translation. I don't know the reason. Are you done with this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I would like to tender it, and if we don't find the document, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Marked for identification, the Serbian version marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2800, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I congratulate on it being a round number, 2800. And can we now look at 1D01659. The English should remain on the monitor, because that is the correct translation for that document. This has been put together erroneously as well. Can we look at page 2. That seems to be the title, the correct title page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, this is a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that in English too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is the 19th of February, 1994. Item 2, "Our forces." What exactly were our forces doing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here units are preparing and carrying out tasks related to moving TMS, technical equipment and materiel, over 12.7 millimetre in calibre. Fuel and food are being resupplied and an inventory, records of equipment that will remain at the positions are being compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is that consistent with your information on agreement compliance and everything that was done afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the activity that ensued once the order had been received on the regrouping of forces. So this is confirms that the order is being implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we please move on to the next page. It's the first page in this document, because the Serbian has two pages only. And in the English document it's paragraph 8, item 8, at the very end of the document. Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, item 8, the third bullet point, our units have -- what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our units have, with maximum effort, taken steps to adhere to the measures ordered with regard to complying with the cease-fire and moving TMS artillery pieces over 12.7 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that in keeping with your information?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is also about a consistent implementation of the agreement. It even goes a step further than that. They're trying to make sure that a cease-fire prevails quite regardless of the fact that in paragraph 1 -- or, rather, the first bullet point here you see that the Muslims are continuing with their engineering work throughout the cease-fire and are continuing to take and capture territory by doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you still remember -- perhaps we should go back to the first page. Is this a secret document? Is it classified?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My answer is whenever you have a combat report, it's always classified to some degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2801, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D00401.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, this is an interim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that's already been admitted as D2517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an interim report concerning the withdrawal of heavy weapons by General Galic. Who is this report for?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's for the President of Republika Srpska and that was you at the time, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, about the civilian authorities in Hadzici trying to get in the way of the implementation of this agreement, specifically the municipal president, Mr. Ratko Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Line 8 in paragraph 2, that same meeting. At that meeting lack of confidence was expressed.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, lack of confidence was expressed in the position that had been taken with it being stressed that the Supreme Command and the corps commander should have submitted an order in writing on the withdrawal and relocation of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the last page.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Despite being urged to respect the recommendations of the Supreme Commander, those from the brigade commands and the SRK were present, were unable to convince him to respect them. End of quote. In this case, the VRS did not have the authority on the ground -- did not have any authority over the local civilian authorities. For that reason, the corps commander addresses the president, pleading with him to use his authority to try and get the local civilian authorities to comply with the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about the Serb part of Hadzici? What was in position vis-a-vis the enemy, and what about the concern expressed here by the civilian authorities? Was that a justified concern or was it simple arrogance?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's leading and outside of the scope of the cross-examination, Your Honours. We never discussed Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a corps and its artillery, and that implies everything within a 20-kilometre radius around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but the -- you should have stopped after "authorities." The last sentence was very much leading. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic? We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The concern felt and expressed by the civilian authorities in Hadzici is perfectly understandable. The Hadzici municipality was in a really difficult spot. The most difficult spot of all, the municipalities within the Sarajevo general area. It was quite isolated to the west, and in the eventuality of a Muslim attack from Mount Igman or from Kiseljak, they would have been entirely unable to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that the number D2517 was marked for identification due to the lack of B/C/S original. So now it's time to admit it full. Do you have any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informed that the English translation in both versions are a bit different. Do you have any suggestion, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would probably invite my colleagues to send this to CLSS for a revised translation. My simple recommendation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no time to check, but perhaps the service itself should check the translation for accuracy. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll use the previous D2517, and we'll add this original to that, and then that will simplify the procedure. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01660. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, here we see another regular combat report dated the 20th of February. Number 2, "Our forces," the second paragraph, please. You don't have to read everything word by word, but just tell us generally what the Main Staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command is telling us about here.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is being reported here is the withdrawal of weapons in keeping with the agreement. As for the weapons that for one reason or the other were not moved, these same weapons were inspected by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about UNPROFOR activities? Paragraph 3 under (a). There was a meeting that was held, and what exactly did UNPROFOR say there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting with the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, General Galic. The Secretary-General's envoy expresses the satisfaction with gratitude to the Serbian side on their efforts to implement the agreement on the withdrawal of artillery pieces. He visited the military barracks and saw for himself that the equipment had been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please press on.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A meeting was held between General Galic and General Soubirou where details of some problems were discussed with regard to the withdrawal, and it was all successfully resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, were the proposals of General Milosevic adopted, General Milosevic and others who invoked caution on the 9th of February?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, the proposals were not adopted, and the agreement was implemented as concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what was the view that ordinary soldiers among their own ranks took regarding that in Hadzici and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all took a dim view of that agreement, because we were afraid of the possibility that the clashes would escalate. Nevertheless, we tried to act as true professionals and comply with everything, every single thing that was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next page, please, and tell us about item 5, morale and security. You don't have to read it out out loud. Just tell us whether it's perfectly consistent with everything that you have yourself been telling us.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's consistent. It reflects the morale among the troops on the ground and how unhappy they were about this withdrawal of weapons, artillery weapons. People were afraid -- were afraid of what that withdrawal might give way to. The ordinary soldiers there saw this as some kind of defeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, I was the person who concluded that agreement. What sort of reputation did I enjoy with the soldiers at the time? How did they see me?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to have to say this, but your reputation was not really the best at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that would mean what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People felt that this was some sort of betrayal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2802, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Given the anger felt by the soldiers and given the caution expressed previously by Mr. Radic, the civilian authorities in Hadzici, given the view that the soldiers took of me at the time, were they justified in feeling this anger? Were the Muslims acting in compliance with the cease-fire or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you're not able to conduct your examination properly, then the Chamber is thinking about asking the counsel to take -- take up your role. Please heed to the advice of the Chamber to refrain from making -- asking leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, was the cease-fire being complied with, the cease-fire that had previously caused us to surrender our weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obvious based on what happened later on that the cease-fire did not spell an end to the war. It was just one of many cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once this cease-fire took effect, it was soon violated by the Muslims, and then the fighting continued.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7033, please. Thank you. Can we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with this document? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the commitments of the agreement that was concluded was to monitor and regularly report on any violations of the cease-fire. This report covers several days during which violations committed by the Muslims occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we please go to page 3 in relation to the 19th and 20th of February. And the agreement had just been signed. So who was in charge of this on a minute-to-minute basis, and who was it who was informed about these violations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was kept by the hour at the corps command. The duty operations officer would receive reports from brigade commanders according to a pre-established schedule. Violation reports would be received and forwarded to the UNPROFOR command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was their reaction to our reports?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally there would be no response from UNPROFOR. Did they do anything about it? Did they speak to the Muslim side about this? I don't really know, but even if that was the case, it certainly led to nothing, because the Muslim violations continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think this is probably the first document in the redirect where Dr. Karadzic asked one kind of question to establish some basis for the witness to be able to comment on the document, and he asked whether he was familiar with it, and although he didn't say -- the witness didn't say specifically how he might be familiar with it, I think he gave enough context for it to be admitted, but I just wanted to put a marker down for any further documents that Dr. Karadzic intends on using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't heard from the witness from where this document was from and who produced it, for what purpose. Do you know, that Mr. Indjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I explained a while ago that the operations duty officer at the corps command was in charge of keeping such documents based on information received from the brigades. This type of document would then be translated and submitted to UNPROFOR for their information so that they would be informed of any cease-fire violations. So this document passed through my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this document was produced by you. It's a compilation of information gathered in such a way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The document was compiled by the duty operations officer at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command. It would then be forwarded by my office to UNPROFOR command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about lines 11 through 14 and page 8? I thought that was sufficiently clear. Seventy-eight, 78. The previous page. At lines 11 through 14, page 78. What is stated there among other things is that the lieutenant-colonel forwarded these reports to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, do you know when this report was written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at this report, it covers the period between the 10th and the 20th of February, 1994. So this was not one of the daily reports. This was part of the agreement to report on any cease-fire violations. So we would take a week or a fortnight, and after a week or a fortnight we would inform UNPROFOR about any cease-fire violations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether you know when this document was written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] February 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, can you show the witness page 29, whatever -- how can a document that was produced in February deals with April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then probably this was an analysis of the entire period and all the violations during that period. It's very difficult for me to answer any questions about the document when I can't see the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you testified earlier on just a minute ago that it is a report passed by you to the UNPROFOR, in answer to the question from myself whether it is a compilation of some information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the report would have been pointless had it not been submitted to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic. Just -- given the position of the Prosecution, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can I just add a codicil to my position. When I answered Your Honour's question, I was raising on the basis of what I had seen in e-court. Subsequent to that, I opened the document in my own e-court and found it to be a 63-page document. The date's up until November 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 37 pages in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you do not object to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, could I have your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't object to the part discussed in court, and for the remainder of the document it's contrary to what the witness has expressly said. On that basis I think it's useful -- no. I don't object to the part that was discussed in court. For the remainder, I think Dr. Karadzic can deal with it with another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is re-examination. I was not going to tender this document through this witness. However, there are suspicions that have been expressed about our actions concerning the withdrawal of artillery weapons and the cease-fire compliance. I sort of took the witness by surprise. He should have been given a chance to go through the document in its entirety because the violations occurred on a daily basis. So I'm not being fair to the witness because I'm not giving him a chance to go through this document. He saw a page dated February, so he was speaking about February. If I had given him the whole document and some time to go through it and see for himself, he would have addressed the document and the entire time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To my memory, the witness has not given us a satisfactory explanation as to the provenance of this document, so I think it's fair enough to admit only those parts commented upon by the witness. I leave it to the Registry in assistance with the parties to indicate what date it was that was commented upon by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 3 in B/C/S. So we'll admit only that page. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2803, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, you can adduce evidence with assistance of other witnesses. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, this was from your corps. Then what about the Main Staff? Were there more comprehensive documents and protests lodged by the Main Staff that might tie in with an overview such as the present document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can Dr. Karadzic be asked to rephrase his question, but maybe there's no point now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did the Main Staff do about this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't respond to that question. As I said, the liaison office for the UN was established at Pale, so all the correspondence through to UNPROFOR went through that liaison office. That being the reason, I'm in no position to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have these daily protests that were submitted to UNPROFOR, but we'll get to that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you were asked some questions about the exchange of prisoners in July and August 1995. Did you ever receive instructions from any officers or VRS commands to avoid the issue of prisoner exchange from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection again. Again it's a leading question. He's suggesting the answers to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I disagree with that. I don't want to state it necessarily in the presence of the witness, but if you read that question, which I wrote and gave it to Dr. Karadzic, that does not suggest either a yes or no answer. The witness is free to answer that question either yes or no, and that is not a leading question in my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will allow the witness to ask -- I'm sorry, allow the accused to ask that question. The Chamber will allow it. Do you remember the question? Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. The issue of the exchange of prisoners was an issue that was dealt with by a government body in charge of prisoner exchanges at the head of which was Dragan Bulajic. I attended the meetings as a liaison officer rather than a member of the exchange commission. I never received personally from anyone any suggestion regarding the issue of the imprisoned -- the persons taken prisoner in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, you attended some meetings. Did you ever observe or notice that the Serb side, which was in charge of the prisoner exchanges, differentiated when it came to exchanges of prisoners from Srebrenica as opposed to any other area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the meetings from 1992 until the end of the war that dealt with prisoner exchanges, in all of them the Serb side always had the same position and that was that prisoners should be exchanged all for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Did you ever observe whether -- or noticed whether the Serb side as opposed [no interpretation] [In English] in comparison to [Interpretation] So the question was: Was there any difference in the treatment of the prisoners from Srebrenica or prisoners that were held by Serbs from other areas?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings which I attended -- at the meetings which I attended, there was never any special treatment of this issue of prisoners from Srebrenica. The position was always that there should be an all-for-all exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You admit that there was a discussion about prisoners from Srebrenica. Can I take your answer to mean that there was actually a discussion about the prisoners from Srebrenica, which is not different from any other previous discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can recall that Amor Masovic asked in one of the meetings that the -- the negotiations should include the persons from Srebrenica. Now, because there was no information, that neither Amor Masovic as a Muslim representative nor anyone from our side had any information about the number of persons from Srebrenica, that issue remained open and no further negotiations were led on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. The question from Mr. Karadzic was whether there's a change in the Serb side as regards the prisoners from Srebrenica, and then you said there's no difference in the treatment of prisoners from Srebrenica. But how -- how can you discuss your -- the treatment of prisoners from Srebrenica if you knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can talk about it because what I'm saying is that the general position was always that any of -- at all of the meetings that the exchange should be all for all. The Srebrenica prisoners were not included in these negotiations because there were never -- there was never any information, specific information, about these people, the numbers, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the Serb side trying to avoid this exchange of prisoners from Srebrenica? That's what the point of my question was when I asked whether there was any difference in their treatment, because in this document it says that Mladic offered that prisoners should be exchanged all for all.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information, I repeat, that there was ever any attempt to avoid discussions of any part of the -- about any part of the territory when it came to prisoner exchanges, and I repeat, the position was always that they should be exchanged all for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, you were going to say something about the role of the liaison officer. Could I now invite you to explain this to us, and especially to point out the positions that the liaison officer puts forth and what the degree of his autonomy is in this in reporting the positions of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again Dr. Karadzic is, in my submission, leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In what part is this question leading?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The degree of autonomy. Inviting him to talk about the degree of autonomy in his reporting vis-a-vis the positions of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, can you restrict your question to this: "Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, you were going to say something about the role of the liaison officer." Can it be kept within those bounds?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So could the witness please now reply to the question as you phrased it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that there is insufficient understanding or a misunderstanding of the role of the liaison officer, and that's why I asked to be allowed to explain it. A liaison officer has absolutely no command role of any kind, nor can he or she take any decisions independently. A liaison officer must consistently report what one party relates to the other, and in addition, in a technical sense, we as liaison officers were duty-bound to forward communications and correspondence, to take part in organising meetings, in monitoring the implementation of certain agreements that were reached. We had to provide constant communication between the Main Staff of the VRS and the UNPROFOR command, to assist in all humanitarian actions including humanitarian convoys, repairs to infrastructures and similar. As a liaison officer, knowing the situation on the ground, I could put forth certain suggestions to my commander, telling him how I saw the situation and propose what he might do, but it was his decision, and my duty was to consistently implement that, his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 14 of today's transcript, you were asked about a meeting at the Jela restaurant and what you knew about crimes. Now, the two generals who were at this meeting, Smith and Mladic, did they discuss, did they talk about this issue, the crimes, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear any mention of any crimes while I was present at the said meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 12 and 13, you said, and you repeated this on several occasions, that you had some 100 communications with Mladic. How did this happen? Was it oral, in writing? Was it face-to-face? So technically speaking, what kind of communications did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the ones that you mentioned. So phone conversations, letters or reports in writing, if it was necessary to put forth a proposal or submit a report, up until going and seeing in person General Mladic at his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you and Mladic talk about crimes? Did you exchange any information about this at the Jela restaurant outside of what was said during the meeting itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, and General Mladic never informed me about things that I did not need in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about certain reports -- or, rather, reporting in the foreign media. Did you have access to the foreign press on a daily basis? Did you receive them? Did you receive the papers that brought those reports and articles that you were shown here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the liaison officer who liaised with UNPROFOR and other members of the international community, and thanks to the fact that I understand English, I was able to get information from the press, the foreign press, and the reports that they published on various issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But have you read any of the articles that were shown to you by Madam Edgerton, by Mr. Block or others about the allegations about the developments after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. The first time I read anything about Srebrenica and learned detailed information about Srebrenica was when I received a Dutch report of many pages which analysed the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was is this, what year?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the accuracy and fairness of reporting of the foreign media?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Their unbiased reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think now, Your Honours, we may be just getting a little bit outside of the scope of cross-examination when we begin to talk about the bias of the media, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not put some news clippings from news media.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I put one report by Mr. Block which the witness said he had not -- sorry. I put one report by Mr. Block and one AP article which the witness said corresponded to and supplemented the evidence he gave in paragraph 171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you also put an AFP clipping as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we might be referring to the same clipping, but perhaps not. I'm not disagreeing with you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer this simply by saying that the general opinion in Republika Srpska was prevailed that the Serbs have lost the media war. It is easy for me to understand why we had lost this media war, because there were war correspondents in Bosnia-Herzegovina and war correspondents need blood and flesh and not us. So all our Serb efforts to end the war and our efforts for peace were not really that interesting. It was necessary to find the places where war was going on and find bloody scenes. So my answer is that I feel that the war correspondents in Bosnia-Herzegovina were generally partial, biased, and that they actually contributed because they were partial in their reporting to the continuation of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 3 it says "us" whereas the witness said "we."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So would you please clarify that. You said that they needed --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't need stories about peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few more questions. Could you tell the Trial Chamber at the time of the events in Srebrenica, were there any other developments, war events, around Sarajevo and in Republika Srpska? What was happening in military terms in those days in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm not sure either how this arises from the cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Karadzic -- just a second. Mr. Karadzic -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I can hear you in my earphones but also in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you explain how it arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I would like to know -- I would like to hear what events were in the focus of Colonel Indjic's interest. Was it Srebrenica alone, and was he supposed to know more about it or not? What all else was happening in military terms? There was expressed a suspicion here about his knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Just a second. You don't have to continue. Point taken. Please continue. Or do you remember the question, Mr. Indjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember the question, although it is hard now to assess all that was happening in the area -- in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but simply put, war was still on, so there was a war going on. As for Srebrenica and everything that relates to Srebrenica, I can only reiterate once again with great certainty that I was never involved in any way, nor did I have any information about Srebrenica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember did Mount Dinara fall, and at what time of the year was it? This was -- this is between us and the Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of all of these final days, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I withdraw that question. The last question: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, do you remember how the international community, the international public opinion, and the UN included, how they treated and dealt with the crisis surrounding Cerska? Could you tell us about it? And could you tell us whether you can see any parallels between the way Srebrenica was treated and Cerska 93?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any views of that. I don't have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Never mind then. Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, transcript page 28 -- 7289, earlier on today in answer -- in answer to the question put by Ms. Edgerton, which was related your knowledge whether there's a claim from the Muslim part or the international community as regards the fate of missing persons from Srebrenica, I'll read out the question: "Even the Bosnian authorities by that point in time, by the 20th of July, 1995, knew that their men in Srebrenica were missing, and you claim you know nothing." And you answered: "I still claim that I didn't know anything and that they did know about it. Of course they did. They organised it themselves." And you -- you were asked to clarify what you meant by "they organised it themselves," and you referred to a meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic in 1993. Now that we heard from you that you came to know about what happened in Srebrenica after reading -- after the war, after reading the NIOD report, et cetera, I really don't understand what you meant, but the Muslims organised it themselves. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will say a few things. In 1993, the leadership of Srebrenica asked Alija Izetbegovic to provide a solution, because Srebrenica could not survive as it was, and Alija Izetbegovic replied decisively that -- that the Americans wanted him to show 3.000 dead so that they could take action against the Serb side. The next thing: Before the Srebrenica operation - and I learned of this late -- Naser Oric, a division commander, and the entire Muslim leadership pulled out of Srebrenica. So they were not there while the -- the Srebrenica operation was in place.
